content: The branch model defines how work flows from a developer's hands into stable software.

RaiSE uses an explicit release-branch model: `main` holds stable, released code; a release branch (e.g. `release/3.1.0`) is the active development integration target; story branches are cut from and merged back to the release branch.
`main` holds stable, released code.
a release branch (e.g. `release/3.1.0`) is the active development integration target
story branches are cut from and merged back to the release branch.
Main receives only tested, released code — stories never branch from or merge to main directly.
The development branch (the current release branch) is the single integration target for all story work. Every story branches from it and merges back to it.
Keeping one integration target avoids the divergence that multiple long-lived branches create.

Story branches follow `story/s{N}.{M}/{slug}`: `s{N}.{M}` identifies the story within its epic, and the slug is a short human-readable description. Consistent naming makes the branch's purpose and parentage legible at a glance.
a short human-readable description
`s{N}.{M}` identifies the story within its epic

Stories merge back through a Merge Request. This is created exclusively via the `/rai-mr-create` skill, and never by manual git push plus a manual glab/gh command, not even for "quick" chore or docs branches.
The `/rai-mr-create` skill is used to create Merge Requests. It runs the full gate suite before pushing and catches drift guards and other non-obvious failures.
The full gate suite is run by the `/rai-mr-create` skill before pushing.
Drift guards are caught by the `/rai-mr-create` skill.

content: Fleet dispatch is the mechanism for parallelizing RaiSE work across multiple concurrent agents. Where a single session executes one body of work at a time, the fleet dispatches several units of work to run simultaneously, each in its own isolated context, and coordinates their completion.
parallelizing RaiSE work across multiple concurrent agents
multiple concurrent agents
each in its own isolated context
Fleet is how RaiSE scales from one human orchestrating one agent toward a few humans orchestrating many agents.
Dispatch launches a unit of work to an agent in the fleet.
Each dispatched unit runs independently — it does not share the orchestrator's context window — so units do not interfere with one another.
The orchestrator decides what to dispatch and to how many agents, then waits for results rather than executing the work itself.
what each agent is doing, what has completed
to coordinate or steer running agents
Status makes the parallel work observable — the orchestrator can see progress across the fleet without reading every agent's full output.
Signals let the orchestrator intervene without restarting a unit.
Units that reach a gate requiring human approval surface that approval to the orchestrator rather than self-approving.
Fleet work still respects governance.
Parallelism increases throughput; it does not relax the HITL and governance discipline that applies to single-session work.
HITL and governance discipline that applies to single-session work.
Units that reach a gate requiring human approval surface that approval to the orchestrator rather than self-approving.

Each fleet unit is isolated (its own context, often its own worktree) so that concurrent work does not collide — no shared mutable state, no context bleed between agents. Isolation is what makes parallelism safe: the cost of an isolated worktree is paid precisely when concurrent agents would otherwise conflict.
Parallelizes work across concurrent, isolated agents
Orchestrator dispatches and waits; it does not execute the dispatched work
Exposes status (observability) and signal (coordination) channels
Governance and HITL still apply — units surface approvals, never self-approve

An automated quality checkpoint that must pass before work proceeds.
A quality floor is where a commit that breaks any gate is not complete, and work never advances below the floor.
Gates make quality a property of the process rather than a matter of individual diligence.
Gates are run exclusively through `rai gate check`.

Direct test invocation (`uv run pytest`, `npm test`) is prohibited: it floods the agent's context window with raw output and bypasses the gate-tracking that records results in the project database for analytics and for blocking on repeated failures.
`rai gate check` is the only sanctioned way to run tests in a RaiSE project. It reads gate configuration from the manifest, scopes output for context efficiency, and records results.

The pipeline engine is the execution backbone of RaiSE. It orchestrates work through an ordered sequence of phases, each phase bound to a skill and optionally to a Human-In-The-Loop (HITL) gate.

The pipeline is the process; the process is the quality system. Phases are never skipped — even for small work — because the structure is what makes the outcome reliable and the governance trail complete.

All code is reviewed before merge. Review is not optional, even for small changes. Every story passes through at minimum an architecture review and a quality review. Both are deliberately adversarial: the reviewer's job is to challenge the implementation and try to find what is wrong, not to validate it or rubber-stamp it. The goal is to surface problems before they reach production, when they are cheap to fix.

Test-Driven Development is mandatory in RaiSE, with no exceptions. The discipline is non-negotiable because tests are the specification of behavior, not a verification afterthought added once code exists. Writing the test first forces the interface and the expected outcome to be decided before implementation details cloud the picture. If behavior is not covered by a test, it is not specified.
Before any production code, write a failing test that defines the expected behavior.
